title: Simulate, Evolve, Validate, Ship: AI-Discovered Algorithms for LLM Serving Stacks
tldr: IBM Research uses a CPU-based simulator of llm-d and vLLM plus an agentic harness to discover serving policies, then validates the winners on GPUs and upstreams them to llm-d. The loop has produced admission control, flow control and LoRA routing plugins for the llm-d router.

key_points.text: Every llm-d subsystem (routing, admission control, flow control, scheduling, prefill/decode, autoscaling) is an open design problem, but GPU experiments take days and cost thousands of dollars, so few ideas get tested.
The loop is simulate, evolve, validate, ship. A human gives only the goal, SLO constraints, workloads and hardware; the output is a production-ready llm-d policy.
The simulator (BLIS) is a digital twin of llm-d and vLLM that runs on CPUs. An agentic harness plans hypotheses, writes algorithms as code, runs them in the simulator and learns across iterations.
Simulation confirms the direction of a gain; real hardware measures its size. Validation turns simulated code and config into llm-d code, deploys it and benchmarks it.

Translation uses three agents: one maps signals between simulator and llm-d (KV cache utilization, queue depth, priority), a writer translates, and a reviewer tests. Agents check each other's work, not their own.
A time-unit mismatch in saturation detection between simulator and llm-d invalidated hours of GPU results. They added pre-deploy parity checks and post-benchmark log checks.
Attaching real benchmark evidence to PRs made upstream review faster. Three policies were merged into the llm-d router: admission gate, flow control and LoRA routing.

The baseline admission gate accepts everything until saturation hits 100%, when queues are already long. The new probabilistic admitter rejects low-priority requests with probability rising with saturation and always accepts critical ones.

The soft reflective ceiling flow-control policy orders admitted requests so critical traffic is never blocked behind low-priority work, slowing low-priority queues as load rises without rejecting anything.
Both are llm-d plugins enabled with a configuration change.

Q&A: a prompted agent with a methodology file forgot to persist algorithms and workloads and made false claims, so they built a harness with deterministic tooling and hypothesis bundles (main, negative, ablation arms).

numbers.text: The simulator runs about 200x faster than real GPU inference.
Validation setup: four H100 GPUs, a Qwen 14B model, eight workloads across four shapes (chatbot, code generation, agentic and others) at various loads.
Probabilistic admission: critical-request TTFT improved by up to 97% and end-to-end latency by up to 50%, at the cost of more low-priority rejections.
Flow-control policy: critical TTFT improved by up to 98%, latency improved by up to 50x, with zero requests rejected.

open_gaps.text: Running the loop continuously against live traffic is the goal but not reached; every step can fail and still needs human review of logs.
llm-d, the simulator and the harness all keep changing, which makes unattended overnight discovery hard.
Sim-to-real translation is error prone; one config mismatch forced discarding a full GPU run.

opportunities.text: Enable the new admission and flow-control plugins in llm-d and compare critical-request TTFT with the baseline under overload.
Use a CPU simulator to screen scheduling or admission policies against SLOs before spending GPU time.
Give coding agents deterministic tooling that forces them to persist algorithms, workloads and results before claiming success.
Attach simulation and real-cluster benchmark evidence to llm-d PRs that change routing or scheduling policies.
